entries.lesson_core_move: Recognize time invariance by interpreting whether delaying or advancing any continuous-time input causes the system output to undergo the identical delay or advance without changing shape or rule.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Meaning of Time Invariance

blocks.text: A continuous-time system is time invariant when shifting the input by $T$ before the system produces the same shift by $T$ at the output after the system. In other words, the system commutes with input shifts: the shape and rule of the output stay the same, and only the time origin moves.
To test the other path, start with the system output $y(t)=S\{x(t)\}$ and then shift that output by the same amount. The result is the system-then-shift path, abbreviated $y_{sts}(t)$.

blocks.latex: y_{sts}(t)=y(t-T), \; \text{compare } y_{tts}(t) \stackrel{?}{=} y_{sts}(t) \text{ for all } t,T

blocks.text: The test is simple: a system is time invariant if the two paths are identical for every input $x(t)$ and every shift $T$. If the shift direction, the shift size, or the output rule changes, the system is not time invariant.

The cleanest base case is the memoryless system $y(t)=x(t)$. For a delay of $T$, both paths give $x(t-T)$, so this is the simplest template for the later matching-delay, matching-advance, and mismatch examples.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Matching Output Delay

example_content.example_prompt: Test time invariance for $y(t)=2x(t-1)$ under input delay $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is an input delay $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$. To test time invariance, keep the system rule fixed as $y(t)=2x(t-1)$ and compare the time-shift-then-system path with the system-then-time-shift path.
Now compute the system-then-shift path from the unshifted output. The internal delay of $1$ stays inside the rule, and the output is shifted by the same amount $T$.
The two expressions are identical term by term: both paths give $2x(t-T-1)$. That means the input delay propagates through the system unchanged.
So this system is time invariant for this delay test. The fixed offset inside $x(t-1)$ does not break shift commutation because both paths still produce the same delayed output.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Matching Output Advance

example_content.example_prompt: Test time invariance for $y(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)$ using an advance input $x_1(t)=x(t+T)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is an advance input $x_1(t)=x(t+T)$. Keep the system rule fixed as $y(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)$ and compare the time-shift-then-system path with the system-then-time-shift path.
Now compute the system-then-shift path from the unshifted output. The output is first $y(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)$, and then it is advanced by the same amount $T$.

The two paths match exactly, so this is a matched output advance. That means the system is time invariant here as well, and the sign change from delay to advance does not change the compare-step method.

sections.section_title: Recognizing When a Shift Changes the Output Pattern

example_content.example_prompt: Check whether $y(t)=t\,x(t)$ is time invariant under input shift $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is an input shift $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$. Keep the system rule fixed as $y(t)=t\,x(t)$ and compare the time-shift-then-system path with the system-then-time-shift path.
Now compute the system-then-shift path from the unshifted output. First the system gives $y(t)=t\,x(t)$, and then the output is delayed by the same amount $T$.
The two paths do not match because the factor of $t$ becomes $t-T$ after the output shift. That means the output pattern changes with the shift, so this system is not time invariant.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the output produced by first shifting a continuous-time input signal and then applying the system rule, so it can be compared against the system-then-shift path in a time-invariance test.

sections.section_title: Introduction to The Shift-Then-System Path

blocks.text: The shift-then-system path is the first leg of a time-invariance test. Start by shifting the input signal first, then apply the same system rule that would act on the original input. For this section, the shifted input is written as $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$.

If the system is written as $\mathcal{S}\{x(t)\}=y(t)$, then the shift-then-system path applies that same rule to the shifted input. Nothing about the system rule changes; only the input argument changes first.

In the simplest base case, if the system rule is just $y(t)=x(t)$, then the shift-then-system path gives $y_{ST}(t)=x(t-T)$. This is the output you will compare against the system-then-shift path in the next step.

sections.section_title: Writing the Shifted Input as the System Input

example_content.example_prompt: For $y(t)=2x(t)$, find the shift-then-system output when $x(t)$ is first shifted by $T$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the system rule is already known: $y(t)=2x(t)$. For the shift-then-system path, first rename the shifted input as $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ so the system sees the shifted signal as its input.
Now apply the same system rule to $x_1(t)$ instead of to $x(t)$. Nothing about the rule changes; only the input has been shifted before the gain is applied.
So the shift-then-system output is $2x(t-T)$. This is the direct substitution result that will be compared against the system-then-shift path in the next step.

sections.section_title: Applying a Memoryless System Rule After the Input Shift

example_content.example_prompt: For $y(t)=x(t-3)$, find the shift-then-system output when $x(t)$ is first shifted by $T$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the internal delay in the system rule: $y(t)=x(t-3)$. Start by writing the shifted input as $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ so the system receives the shifted signal as its input.
Now apply the same rule to the shifted input. Because the system delays whatever input it sees by $3$, substitute $x_1$ into the rule to get the shift-then-system output.
So the shift-then-system output is $x((t-T)-3)$. The only new move is the substitution of the shifted input into the system's internal delay.

sections.section_title: Applying a System Rule with Internal Input Shifts After the Input Shift

example_content.example_prompt: For $y(t)=x(t-3)$, find the shift-then-system output when $x(t)$ is first shifted by $T$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the internal delay in the system rule: $y(t)=x(t-3)$. Start by writing the shifted input as $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ so the system receives the shifted signal as its input.
Now apply the same rule to the shifted input. Because the system delays whatever input it sees by $3$, substitute the shifted input into the rule and keep the parentheses in order.
So the shift-then-system output is $x((t-T)-3)$. The only new move is the substitution of the shifted input into the system's internal delay.

sections.section_title: Applying a Multi-Term System Rule After the Input Shift

example_content.example_prompt: For $y(t)=3x(t-1)+2x(t+1)-5x(t)$, compute $y_{STS}(t)$ after $x(t)$ is first shifted by $T$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a multi-term linear rule: each term uses $x(t)$ with a different internal time shift, but the coefficients stay fixed. Start by writing the shifted input as $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ so the system sees the shifted signal as its input.
Now substitute $x_1$ into every occurrence of $x(\cdot)$ in the system rule. Keep the constants $3$, $2$, and $-5$ unchanged while shifting only the time arguments inside each term.

So the shift-then-system output is $3x((t-T)-1)+2x((t-T)+1)-5x(t-T)$. The pattern is the same in every term: shift the input first, then replace each $x(\cdot)$ with the shifted input without changing the coefficients.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the system-then-shift path by applying the continuous-time system rule to x(t) to get y(t), then replacing t with t - T to form y(t - T) for comparison in a time-invariance test.

sections.section_title: Introduction to The System-Then-Shift Path

blocks.text: The system-then-shift path means you first apply the system rule to the original input $x(t)$ to get a finished output $y(t)$, and then you shift that completed output by replacing every $t$ with $t-T$.
That shift acts on the completed expression, not on the input first. So the $t$ inside $x(t-a)$ shifts with the rest of the output, while the constant term $B$ stays the same.
So if you already have $y(t)$, the system-then-shift path is just $y(t-T)$. This is the output that will later be compared with the result of shifting the input first in a time-invariance test.

sections.section_title: Applying the System Rule Before Any Input Shift

example_content.example_prompt: For the system $y(t)=2x(t)+x(t-1)$ and input $x(t)=t^2$, find $y(t)$ and then compute $y(t-T)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the system rule is already given, so the first job is to apply it to the original input $x(t)=t^2$ and form the finished output $y(t)$ before any shift is introduced.
Now the system-then-shift path shifts the completed output, not the input rule. That means every explicit $t$ in $y(t)$ is replaced by $t-T$, while the constant term stays unchanged.

This example shows the order clearly: first build $y(t)$ from $x(t)$, then shift that finished expression to get $y(t-T)$. That is the system-then-shift path used later in the time-invariance comparison.

sections.section_title: Forming y(t - T) from a Direct Output Expression

example_content.example_prompt: If $y(t)=5t^2-2t+1$, write $y(t-T)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the output is already finished, so the only job is to replace every explicit $t$ in $y(t)$ with $t-T$ and leave constants unchanged.
Now simplify the substituted expression by expanding the square and collecting like terms. The constant $1$ stays fixed because it is not attached to $t$.
This is the system-then-shift form for a direct output expression: start with $y(t)$, replace $t$ by $t-T$ everywhere it appears, and then simplify the result.

sections.section_title: Forming y(t - T) When y(t) Contains x(t - a)

example_content.example_prompt: If $y(t)=x(t-2)+3x(t)$, write $y(t-T)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the output already contains delayed input terms, so the only task is to shift the finished output expression by replacing $t$ with $t-T$ everywhere it appears.
The embedded delay stays attached to the shifted time, so $x(t-2)$ becomes $x(t-T-2)$ and the undelayed term $x(t)$ becomes $x(t-T)$.
This shows the same system-then-shift rule in a delayed-output setting: shift the completed output, keep each delay attached to its argument, and write the result in simplified form.

sections.section_title: Forming y(t - T) When y(t) Combines Multiple Terms

example_content.example_prompt: If $y(t)=2x(t-1)-x(t)+t+4$, write $y(t-T)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the output mixes delayed input terms, an undelayed input term, an explicit $t$ term, and a constant, so the shift must be applied to every $t$-dependent part exactly once.
The delayed input term becomes $x(t-T-1)$, the undelayed input term becomes $x(t-T)$, the explicit time term becomes $t-T$, and the constant $4$ stays unchanged.
This is the same system-then-shift rule in a mixed-expression setting: shift the finished output once, carry every $t$-bearing term with the shift, and leave constants alone.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compare the shift-then-system and system-then-shift expressions for an arbitrary input shift to classify a continuous-time input-output system as time invariant or time varying.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Testing Time Invariance

blocks.text: To test time invariance, compare two paths for the same input shift $T$: shift the input first and then apply the system, or apply the system first and then shift the output by the same $T$. The object to recognize is the pair of expressions that should match if the system preserves shifts without changing its rule.

The first path is the shift-then-system path: start with the shifted input $x(t-T)$, feed it into the system, and name the result $y_1(t)$. For the simplest base case, this is the path that shows what the system does after the delay has already been built into the input.

The second path is the system-then-shift path: first compute the output $y(t)=T\{x(t)\}$, then replace $t$ with $t-T$ to form the shifted output $y_2(t)$. Written directly, this is the same as taking the output rule and evaluating it at the delayed time.

The decision rule is simple: if the simplified expressions for $y_1(t)$ and $y_2(t)$ are exactly the same for every valid $T$, the system is time invariant. In the base identity case $y(t)=x(t)$, both paths reduce to $x(t-T)$, so the matching rule is easy to see before any harder examples appear.
This section sets up the comparison strategy only; later sections will reuse the same notation to test specific system rules and decide whether the paths match or fail to match after simplification.

sections.section_title: Matching Shift-Then-System and System-Then-Shift Expressions

example_content.example_prompt: For $y(t)=2x(t)$, compute the shift-then-system and system-then-shift expressions and decide if they are equal.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is a constant-gain system: multiplying by $2$ should not change the shape of the signal when the input is delayed. To test that, start by shifting the input by $T$ and then pass that shifted input through the system.
That first path is the shift-then-system path. The input becomes $x(t-T)$ first, and the system rule $y(t)=2x(t)$ turns it into $y_1(t)=2x(t-T)$ with the delay preserved inside the argument.
Now take the system-then-shift path. Apply the system to the original input first, which gives $y(t)=2x(t)$, and then shift that output by the same $T$.

The delayed output has the same simplified form as the shift-then-system path, so the two expressions match exactly: $y_1(t)=y_2(t)=2x(t-T)$. Since the two paths are identical for arbitrary $T$, this system is time invariant.

sections.section_title: Nonmatching Shift-Then-System and System-Then-Shift Expressions

example_content.example_prompt: For $y(t)=x(t)+t$, compute the shift-then-system and system-then-shift expressions for an arbitrary shift $T$ and identify the term that prevents them from matching.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the explicit $t$ term in the output rule. Start with the shifted input $x(t-T)$, then apply the system rule at time $t$.
Now apply the system first, then shift the entire output by $T$. The input part shifts the same way, but the added time term must also be evaluated at the shifted time.
Compare the two expressions term by term. The input-dependent parts match, but the explicit-time terms differ: $t$ in $y_1(t)$ and $t-T$ in $y_2(t)$.
Because the two paths do not match for arbitrary $T$, the system is time varying.

sections.section_title: Testing Equality for an Arbitrary Input Shift

example_content.example_prompt: For $y(t)=t\,x(t-2)$, simplify both paths $y_1(t)=T\{x(t-T)\}$ and $y_2(t)=T\{x(t)\}|_{t\to t-T}$ to test equality.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the time prefactor $t$ multiplying the shifted input $x(t-2)$. Start by shifting the input first, then apply the system rule at time $t$.
Now apply the system first, then shift the whole output by $T$. The shifted output inherits the same input argument change, but the prefactor also shifts from $t$ to $t-T$.
Compare the two expressions term by term. The shifted input argument matches, but the coefficients do not: $t$ in $y_1(t)$ versus $t-T$ in $y_2(t)$.
Because the two paths disagree for arbitrary $T$, this system is time varying.

sections.section_title: Classifying Time Invariance from Simplified Path Expressions

example_content.example_prompt: Use the following path expressions and classify the system: $y_1(t)=x(t-T+1)$, $y_2(t)=x(t-T+1)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both paths are already simplified. At this point, the job is to compare the final symbolic forms for exact equality for arbitrary $T$.
Read the two expressions term by term. The shifted argument is identical, and there are no extra coefficients or time offsets that change one path relative to the other.
Because the simplified path expressions match exactly for arbitrary $T$, the system is time invariant.
This is the decision rule for the lesson: if the two simplified paths are identical for every input shift, classify the system as time invariant.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the time-invariance shift test to memoryless continuous-time system rules by verifying that the fixed pointwise mapping from x(t) to y(t) commutes with input shifts and contains no explicit dependence on t.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time-Invariant Memoryless Systems

blocks.text: A continuous-time system is time invariant when shifting the input by $T$ shifts the output by the same $T$ without changing the rule itself. For a memoryless system, the output at each time depends only on the input at that same time, so the pointwise mapping can be written as $y(t)=f(x(t))$.

Start from the shifted input $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$ and apply the same pointwise rule to it. The shifted-input output is $y_T(t)=f(x(t-T))$, so the test is whether this matches the original output shifted by $T$.

The comparison path is system then shift: first form $y(t)=f(x(t))$, then replace $t$ with $t-T$ to get $y(t-T)=f(x(t-T))$. When the two paths agree, the memoryless rule is time invariant, and the simplest base case to remember is a constant-gain rule such as $y(t)=a x(t)$, which clearly gives the same shifted output on both paths.

sections.section_title: Testing a Constant-Gain Memoryless Rule

example_content.example_prompt: Decide whether $y(t)=3x(t)$ is time invariant by comparing the output from $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$ with $y(t-T)$ from the original output.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the shift test on the constant-gain memoryless rule $y(t)=3x(t)$. The shifted input is $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$, so the goal is to compare the shifted-input path with the same rule applied before the shift.
Apply the rule directly to the shifted input. Because the gain is fixed at $3$, the shifted-input path gives $y_T(t)=3x(t-T)$.
Now apply the rule first and shift the output afterward. From $y(t)=3x(t)$, replacing $t$ with $t-T$ gives $y(t-T)=3x(t-T)$, which matches the shifted-input path exactly.

Since both paths produce the same expression, the rule is time invariant. This constant-gain case is the clean base case to reuse before testing nonlinear or explicitly time-dependent memoryless rules.

sections.section_title: Testing a Squaring Memoryless Rule

example_content.example_prompt: Decide whether $y(t)=x^2(t)$ is time invariant by comparing the output from $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$ with $y(t-T)$ from the original output.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the pointwise square rule $y(t)=x^2(t)$, so test it with the same input shift $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$ and compare the shifted-input path to the shifted original output.
Apply the square rule directly to the shifted input. Because the rule is fixed and pointwise, the shifted-input path gives $y_T(t)=(x(t-T))^2$.
Now apply the rule first and shift the output afterward. From $y(t)=x^2(t)$, replacing $t$ with $t-T$ gives $y(t-T)=(x(t-T))^2$.
Both paths match exactly, so the square rule is time invariant. The key distinction is that the rule is nonlinear, but it still commutes with the shift because it has no explicit $t$ dependence.

sections.section_title: Testing a Constant-Offset Memoryless Rule

example_content.example_prompt: Decide whether $y(t)=x(t)+5$ is time invariant by comparing the output from $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$ with $y(t-T)$ from the original output.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the shift test on the additive memoryless rule $y(t)=x(t)+5$. The cue is the fixed output offset $+5$, so the comparison is between the shifted-input path and the output obtained by shifting the original result.
Apply the rule directly to the shifted input. Because the offset is constant, the shifted-input path gives $y_T(t)=x(t-T)+5$.
Now apply the rule first and shift the output afterward. From $y(t)=x(t)+5$, replacing $t$ with $t-T$ gives $y(t-T)=x(t-T)+5$.

Both paths produce the same expression, so the constant-offset rule is time invariant. The important point is that the $5$ is fixed and does not introduce any explicit $t$ dependence when the input is shifted.

sections.section_title: Spotting Explicit Time Dependence in a Memoryless Rule

example_content.example_prompt: Decide whether $y(t)=t x(t)$ is time invariant by comparing the output from $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$ with $y(t-T)$ from the original output.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the explicit time factor $t$ in the memoryless rule $y(t)=t x(t)$. Use the shift test by comparing the shifted-input path with the output obtained after shifting the original result.
Apply the rule to the shifted input first. The shifted-input path is $y_T(t)=t x(t-T)$, because the factor $t$ stays attached to the current time variable.
Now apply the rule first and shift the output afterward. From $y(t)=t x(t)$, replacing $t$ with $t-T$ gives $y(t-T)=(t-T)x(t-T)$.

The two paths do not match, so the rule is not time invariant. The important distinction is that the system is still memoryless, but the explicit $t$ dependence changes under a shift and breaks the commutation test.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compare the shift-then-system and system-then-shift outputs for system rules containing explicit $t$ to recognize when absolute-time dependence makes a continuous-time system time varying.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time-Varying Systems with Explicit $t$

blocks.text: To test time invariance, compare the output of the shifted input, $T(x(t-t_0))$, with the shifted version of the original output, $y(t-t_0)$, where $T(x(t))=y(t)$. If those two paths agree for every shift $t_0$, the system is time invariant.

An explicit $t$ in the system rule means the rule depends on absolute time, not just on the input value. In the simplest case, if $T(x(t)) = t \, x(t)$, then shifting the input gives $T(x(t-t_0)) = t \, x(t-t_0)$, while shifting the original output gives $y(t-t_0) = (t-t_0) \, x(t-t_0)$.

Because $t$ stays tied to the absolute observation time, the two outputs are different in general. That is the key cue: when the system rule contains explicit $t$, the shift test can fail because the output does not move exactly with the input.

sections.section_title: Comparing Paths for a Time-Dependent Multiplier

example_content.example_prompt: For $T(x(t))=t x(t)$ and input $x(t)$, compare the outputs for the shifted input $x(t-t_0)$ and for the shifted original output $y(t-t_0)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the original rule $T(x(t))=t x(t)$, so the unshifted output is $y(t)=t x(t)$. The shift test compares two paths: first shift the input and then apply the system, or first apply the system and then shift the output.

If we shift the input first, the rule uses the current time variable $t$ exactly as written, so the output is $T(x(t-t_0))=t x(t-t_0)$. If we shift the original output instead, we replace $t$ by $t-t_0$ everywhere in $y(t)$, which gives $y(t-t_0)=(t-t_0)x(t-t_0)$.

The mismatch is in the multiplier: one path keeps $t$, while the other changes it to $t-t_0$. That difference means the output does not shift along with the input, so this explicit-$t$ rule is time varying.

sections.section_title: Comparing Paths for a Time-Dependent Offset

example_content.example_prompt: For $T(x(t))=x(t)+t$ and input $x(t)$, compare $T(x(t-t_0))$ with $y(t-t_0)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the original rule $T(x(t))=x(t)+t$, so the unshifted output is $y(t)=x(t)+t$. For the shift test, compare the output of the shifted input with the shifted version of the original output.

If we shift the input first, the system rule becomes $T(x(t-t_0))=x(t-t_0)+t$. If we shift the original output instead, we replace $t$ by $t-t_0$ everywhere in $y(t)$, which gives $y(t-t_0)=x(t-t_0)+(t-t_0)$.

The input term matches on both paths, but the added time term does not. That mismatch is the cue: when the rule contains an explicit $t$ in an offset, the output depends on absolute time, so the system is time varying.

sections.section_title: Tracking Explicit $t$ Through an Input Shift

example_content.example_prompt: For $T(x(t))=t x(t)+x(t)$ and input $x(t)$, compare $T(x(t-t_0))$ with $y(t-t_0)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the original rule $T(x(t))=t x(t)+x(t)$, so the unshifted output is $y(t)=t x(t)+x(t)$. For the shift test, compare the output of the shifted input with the shifted version of the original output, term by term.

If we shift the input first, the rule still uses absolute time $t$ in the multiplier, so $T(x(t-t_0))=t x(t-t_0)+x(t-t_0)$. If we shift the original output instead, we replace every $x(t)$ by $x(t-t_0)$ and every free $t$ by $t-t_0$, which gives $y(t-t_0)=(t-t_0)x(t-t_0)+x(t-t_0)$.
The input term $x(t-t_0)$ matches on both paths, but the multiplier changes from $t$ to $t-t_0$. That mismatch is the cue that the rule depends on absolute time, so the system is time varying.

sections.section_title: Classifying Explicit-$t$ System Rules as Time Varying

example_content.example_prompt: For $T(x(t))=t x(t)+2x(t)$ and input $x(t)$, compare the two shift paths and decide whether the system is time varying.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the original rule $T(x(t))=t x(t)+2x(t)$, so the unshifted output is $y(t)=t x(t)+2x(t)$. To classify the rule, compare the shifted-input path with the shifted-output path and check whether the expressions match.

If we shift the input first, the system rule gives $T(x(t-t_0))=t x(t-t_0)+2x(t-t_0)$. If we shift the original output instead, we replace every $x(t)$ by $x(t-t_0)$ and every free $t$ by $t-t_0$, so $y(t-t_0)=(t-t_0)x(t-t_0)+2x(t-t_0)$.
The $2x(t)$ term shifts cleanly, but the multiplier changes from $t$ to $t-t_0$. Because the two paths are not the same, the rule is time varying.

entries.lesson_core_move: Distinguish time invariance from signal shifting by tracing the shift-then-system and system-then-shift paths to decide whether a continuous-time system preserves input delays as identical output delays.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Invariance vs. Signal Shifting

blocks.text: Signal shifting means moving one waveform in time. Delay the input by $\tau$ with $x(t-\tau)$, and advance it by $\tau$ with $x(t+\tau)$; this is a shift in the argument, not a change in signal shape.

Time invariance is the property that a continuous-time system preserves that same shift at the output. Compare two paths: first shift the input and then apply the system, versus applying the system first and shifting the output afterward.

Use this test rule: let $y(t)=T\{x(t)\}$, then form $T\{x(t-\tau)\}$ and compare it to $y(t-\tau)$. If the expressions are identical for all $\tau$ and for the same $x(t)$, the system is time invariant.
The goal is identical delay propagation: the output must be delayed (or advanced) by the same amount and in the same direction, with no additional algebraic change beyond that shift.

sections.section_title: Identifying Signal Shifting as an Operation on One Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Given the signal $x(t)$, interpret the shifted inputs $x(t-3)$ and $x(t+2)$ as delayed or advanced versions of the same waveform before any system is applied.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the cue from the prompt: the core input is $x(t)$, and the only change shown is a substituted time argument. First, identify the unshifted reference signal as $x(t)$.
Read $x(t-3)$ as $x(t)$ delayed by $3$ in time, so its feature at time $t$ now appears at $t-3$. Read $x(t+2)$ as $x(t)$ advanced by $2$, so its feature at time $t$ now appears at $t+2$.

This operation only changes the argument value where the same waveform is sampled. The signal rule and shape are preserved; the rule is still the same $x(\cdot)$ relation to time, with horizontal placement shifted.
Keep this distinction separate from system-level claims: at this step, we are only classifying the input expression. A time-invariance test comes next, after a system rule is introduced.

sections.section_title: Comparing the Shift-Then-System and System-Then-Shift Paths

example_content.example_prompt: For the system $T\{x(t)\}=x^2(t)$, compare the output for the shifted input $x(t-\tau)$ with the shifted original output $y(t-\tau)$ when $y(t)=T\{x(t)\}$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the original output $y(t)=x^2(t)$. The time-invariance test asks whether shifting the input first gives the same result as shifting this output by the same amount.
For the shift-then-system path, replace $x(t)$ by $x(t-\tau)$ inside the rule. That gives $T\{x(t-\tau)\}=x^2(t-\tau)$.
For the system-then-shift path, shift the finished output $y(t)$ by the same amount. Replacing $t$ with $t-\tau$ in $y(t)=x^2(t)$ gives $y(t-\tau)=x^2(t-\tau)$.
The two paths produce the same expression, so the input delay is preserved at the output. That is exactly what it means for the system to be time invariant.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Preserved Delays as Time-Invariant Behavior

example_content.example_prompt: For the system $T\{x(t)\}=x(t)+x(t-1)$ and input $x(t-\tau)$, show that the output is exactly the delayed version of the original output.

explanation_blocks.text: Start by writing the original output. The rule adds the current input and a one-unit delayed copy, so the output is $y(t)=x(t)+x(t-1)$.
Now apply the system to the shifted input $x(t-\tau)$. Replace $x(t)$ everywhere in the rule by $x(t-\tau)$, which gives the shift-then-system output.
Next shift the original output by the same amount. Replacing $t$ with $t-\tau$ in $y(t)=x(t)+x(t-1)$ gives the system-then-shift output.
The two expressions are identical term by term, so the delay is preserved by the system. That preserved-delay match is the signature of time-invariant behavior.

sections.section_title: Rejecting Time Invariance from a Single Shifted Output

example_content.example_prompt: For the system $T\{x(t)\}=t\,x(t)$, compare the output for $x(t-\tau)$ with $y(t-\tau)$ and show the paths do not match.

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the original output $y(t)=t\,x(t)$. The time-invariance test asks whether shifting the input produces exactly the same delay on the output and nothing else changes.
For the shift-then-system path, replace $x(t)$ by $x(t-\tau)$ inside the rule. The factor $t$ stays tied to the current time, so the shifted-input output is $T\{x(t-\tau)\}=t\,x(t-\tau)$.
For the system-then-shift path, shift the finished output by the same amount. Replacing $t$ with $t-\tau$ in $y(t)=t\,x(t)$ gives $y(t-\tau)=(t-\tau)\,x(t-\tau)$.
The two expressions are not equal because one path keeps the factor $t$ while the other changes it to $t-\tau$. Since the delay is not preserved exactly, the system is not time invariant.
